extracted.intended_audience: poets, rhetoricians, literary critics, and writers interested in producing the sublime and beautiful (and authors of political/public prose)
extracted.subtask_short: writing for the sublime and beautiful
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for using words, tone, and composition to produce effects of the sublime and beautiful in poetry and rhetoric; also practical norms for clear, moderate political/public prose. Focuses on how words operate (types, effects, combinations) and on desirable/undesirable rhetorical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of words: aggregate, simple abstract, compound abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Words divide into three sorts: (1) aggregate words representing many simple ideas united by nature (man, horse, tree, castle); (2) simple abstract words standing for one simple idea (red, blue, round); (3) compound abstract words formed by an arbitrary union of the others and relations (virtue, honor, persuasion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which class a word belongs to because each class operates differently in producing effects; this classificatory awareness should inform diction and how a poet or speaker expects a word to move an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of compound-abstract words: operate by sound and habit, not by image
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound abstracts (honor, justice, liberty, etc.) produce the sound of the word and the affection in the soul, but not a clear picture or precise idea of the things they stand for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compound-abstract words knowing they often act as powerful mere sounds tied to occasions/habit. They can move the passions without conjuring detailed images; expect them to function through associative force rather than descriptive precision. Beware that overuse without occasion leads to empty rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: General words taught before particular ideas (risk and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most general words (virtue, vice, good, evil) are taught before particular modes of action are presented; thus they can instill dispositions (love/abhorrence) before concrete understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with general terms: they can create strong dispositions or confused ideas when not grounded in particulars. In rhetoric, pairing them with warm tone or appropriate occasions increases affect; used carelessly they yield bombast or contradiction between professed sentiment and particular action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three effects of words: sound, picture, and affection
rubrics_metrics.description: When words affect the hearer they may produce (1) the sound, (2) the picture/representation of the thing signified, and (3) the affection (emotion) of the soul. Different word-classes vary in their capacity to produce these effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design language with awareness which of these three effects you intend to produce. Compound abstracts tend toward sound+affection, simple abstracts can produce all three, aggregates most readily produce all three. You need not always aim for picture—sound and affection alone can be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words can affect without raising images
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary conversation and reading, people are often affected by words without forming images of the things they denote (examples: blind poet Blacklock, blind mathematician Saunderson). Poetry's power does not depend on exciting sensible images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on vivid visual imagery to move readers; well-chosen words and combinations can evoke feeling and effect without pictorial detail. Recognize the role of habit, association, and verbal convention in producing emotion even when no mental picture is formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is not strictly imitative; descriptive poetry works by substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry, especially descriptive poetry, operates chiefly by substitution—words as conventional representatives of realities—rather than strict imitation as in painting or purely dramatic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing descriptive verse, favor the representational and associative power of language over attempting literal imitation of sensory appearance. Understand the difference between dramatic imitation (showing passions in action) and descriptive substitution (evoking effects via words).

rubrics_metrics.name: How words influence the passions (three causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words influence passions chiefly because (1) we share sympathy with others and are affected by tokens of their passions (and words convey those tokens); (2) words can represent affecting things that rarely occur in reality (war, death, heaven/hell); (3) words allow combinations of circumstances that enliven simple objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit these mechanisms: cultivate sympathetic voice, conjure powerful concepts not commonly present, and combine circumstances/terms to generate new, stronger effects than isolated images could. Use combinations and circumspection to build surprise and magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish clear expression from strong expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear expression regards understanding; a strong expression pertains to the passions. They are frequently confounded but are different—languages prized for clarity may lack strength of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your primary aim is to inform (favor clarity) or to move (favor strength). When seeking the sublime or to move passion, prioritize strong expression—choice of weighty words, passionate constructions, and emotive disposition—even if some literal clarity is sacrificed; but avoid incomprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tone and impassioned delivery to convey feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a moving tone of voice, impassioned countenance, and gesture which affect independently of the things about which they are exerted; similarly, words and certain dispositions of words—when associated with passion—move us more than clearer description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In spoken rhetoric or performed poetry, attend to delivery (tone, pace, emphasis) as a primary vehicle of affect. In written work, emulate passionate dispositions through diction, rhythm, and structure to convey contagious feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast: require propriety and coherence in affecting language
rubrics_metrics.description: When affecting words sacred to great occasions are put together without rational view or proper agreement, the style is called bombast; combining them indiscriminately increases force but sacrifices propriety and sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against piling affecting words without rational relation or occasion. Maintain propriety and good sense when assembling high diction; otherwise the effect becomes ludicrous or hollow. Use affecting terms with appropriate context and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accumulation and climactic union to heighten the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: A union or accumulation of well-chosen circumstances (lists culminating in a decisive term) can create a greater sublime than isolated description (examples: Milton's lists ending with 'of Death' and 'a universe of death').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ enumerations, accumulations, and climactic punctuation to concentrate force—build a sequence of items and cap them with a decisive, amplifying term to produce heightened effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words to add conceptual or moral force beyond visual representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Words can annex ideas that painting cannot supply (e.g., adding 'of the Lord' to a painted angel) and thereby increase emotional and sublimity effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the uniquely verbal capacity to name, qualify, or conceptually frame an image to confer moral, religious, or metaphysical weight that visual detail alone cannot supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain facts and unvarnished statement for public political accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain facts, not extended elaborate reasoning or colored eloquence, are more suitable when setting forth public services and administrative achievements; facts 'neither extended by elaborate reasoning, nor heightened by the coloring of eloquence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In political or public writing that aims to persuade on governance or record accomplishments, emphasize clear factual statements and restraint in rhetorical embellishment to increase credibility and public utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a sober, moderate tone in partisan/public political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Those legally invested with public trust should take a decided part but a sober one; party action must be circumscribed by decorum and balanced by temper, avoiding excessive bitterness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing as a public actor or addressing civic matters, frame arguments with moderation and decorum. Passion is permissible, but avoid rancor and unmeasured invective that undermine persuasive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent in purpose and avoid needless obscurity or over-involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition should not be so involved that it is difficult to comprehend the author's meaning; obfuscation betrays design to mislead or to produce alarm (critique of 'The Present State of the Nation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure political critique and argument with clear, fathomable intent. Expose the author's design succinctly and avoid overly complicated diction or tangled presentation that prevents readers from discerning purpose and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not recycle stale controversies or contradictory arguments; prefer useful, just criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid hauling out old, ten-times-repeated arguments, contradictions set against one another, and commonplace laments that add bulk without weight; criticism should attribute causes justly and usefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing polemic or critique, beware of merely reprinting worn material for effect. Target real causes, offer useful diagnoses, and avoid assembling contradictions and commonplace complaints solely to alarm or enlarge the work's apparent importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid doleful, sermon-like composition and 'pious frauds' in public writing
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition resembling a funeral sermon—piteously doleful, nodding to dulness, stored with pious frauds—is counterproductive and more for private advantage than public edification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write public/political argumentation with liveliness, reasoned argument, and honest presentation; avoid overwrought plaintiveness, sentimental fraud, or moralistic posturing intended to manipulate rather than inform.
